subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE

speechtext:
The House resumed from Thursday, May 1, the debate on the motion of Hon. J. A. Robb (Acting Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Woodsworth.
Mr. R. V. LeSUEUR (West Lambton): Mr. Speaker, our discussions of the national budget sometimes, perhaps too often, entail comments and criticisms, which at times become rather severe, but in all cases the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) should know that the arduousness of his task, the weight of the burden and the difficulty involved in the duties of his office, are fully and constantly appreciated by this House. This year the budget aroused unusual interest, both in this chamber and out of it, and upon that the Acting Minister of Finance is to be congratulated. Within the House it commanded that respect which the most important financial statement of the
The Budget-Mr. LeSueur

year merits; in the country it has drawn to itself an unusually alert attention. There, it is every day becoming more generally recognized that this budget inaugurates a new policy on the part of the government, inaugurates a departure from this policy of tariff stability announced by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) last year, and that a responsible minister of the Crown has openly announced that he hopes this budget will prove the death knell of protection. If I rightly interpret the sentiment expressed in a number of orations made by hon. members to my left, they appear to have reason to hope that the changes and alterations in the tariff are not at an end, but that they will continue from year to year during the life of this parliament. The suddenness and the radical nature of this change on the part of the government are, I believe, causing widespread uncertainty ,as to whether the future actions of this government will not be largely influenced, perhaps dominated by, the tenets and dictates of the Progressive party rather than by the old-time principles of Laurier-Fielding Liberalism. Such a budget, Sir, should have a careful analysis in the light of present-day conditions. That analysis, I submit, should not be confined to conditions as they exist within Canada, but should include also a review of world conditions. We do not live unto ourselves alone, and a reasonably accurate knowledge of conditions both within and without Canada and of the general trend of industrial world events is essential to a correct estimate of the changes proposed in the tariff.
Turning to the budget itself and examining it, we find that the Acting Minister of Finance has arranged it in three main divisions. In the first division he discusses the financial condition of Canada; in the second he outlines Canada's trade position as evidenced by her foreign trade; and then, proceeding, I assume, on the conclusions arrived at in these two divisions, he comes to the third division, which deals with the changes he proposes in our tariff policy. I will endeavour in my remarks to adhere more or less to this order.
The first division, namely, that relating to Canada's financial position, has already been fairly well discussed and I will but briefly comment on it in passing. The Acting Minister of Finance pointe/i out that we have, for the fiscal year ending March 31, 1924, an estimated surplus out of ordinary r.evenue of approximately $20,800,000, and that this, together with an income from other sources of about $9,600,000, will give us a total of 
some $30,400,000 to be applied in the reduction of the national debt. The budget also points out, however, that the loan of $50,000,000, made on behalf of the Canadian National Railways and guaranteed by the government, has been so treated as not to affect or influence this result. It has already been pointed out in this discussion that, according to the system of bookkeeping in vogue prior to this year, that loan would be considered as part of our national debt and as a national obligation. But whether we accept the system of bookkeeping adopted this year or adhere to the system in vogue hitherto, is more or less a matter of accounting and does not alter the facts-and it is a fact,-that the Canadian National Railways could not, apart from the government, have secured a loan of $50,000,000 on reasonably good terms, possibly not at all, and that the investors who made that loan looked to the government of this Dominion and not to the Canadian National Railways for the repayment of their interest and principal. It i3 also a matter of common knowledge that the Canadian National Railways are to-day much over-capitalized, that their physical value is much less than their book value as carried on the ledgers of this government, and it would be a delusion and a snare to increase that book value, already too high. Whether we treat that money as being turned into capital, or into maintenance, or into deficit, it is as a matter of fact being handed over to a railroad already too highly capitalized which cannot pay the interest on the debts already incurred and which cannot for many years, possibly not during our life time, be in a position to have its assets offset it liabilities. In short, the asset, if any, which we acquire is certainly non-active, while the obligation assumed is most distinctly and strikingly active, as will be proved every interest day. Therefore, the only safe and sound course is to acknowledge that, so far as the investors are concerned and so far as we are concerned, we have assumed an obligation of $50,000,000 which cannot be eliminated by any process of bookkeeping or be altered by placing it, as it were, in suspense account as an indirect liability. Of course, the amount of money which still remains in the hands of the government from that loan is an asset. Then, considering this loan as a national obligation, and endeavouring to keep ourselves as close to the facts as we can, I ask, do we realize that Canada has since March 31, 1921, added to its national debt by the sum of approximately $118,000,000, while the country to the south of us has in the same period wiped out and eliminated from its debt $1,860,000,000?

The Budget-Mr. LeSaeur
Great Britain in the same period has likewise eliminated from her debt a very considerable sum-I see by their recent budget, this totals £960,000,000 since 1918.
Now., turning to the second division of the budget speech, namely, that relating to Canadian trade, we find it there set out that Canada's commodity trade balance has advanced from an adverse balance in 1914 and in 1921 to a favourable trade balance of approximately $160,000,000 for last year. This result is most gratifying to all Canadians, but it would be neither wise nor businesslike on our part to jump to the too hasty conclusion that therefore Canada is enjoying a period of prosperity; and, whether or not the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) intended this inference to be drawn, several speakers who have followed him in this debate do appear to have drawn that conclusion. It is most important in my opinion that this House, as a deliberative body, considering the fiscal policy for this country should have as accurate ,a knowledge of conditions both within and without Canada as is possible, in order to enable them to properly estimate the changes proposed. The facilities for gathering data, and the science of gauging a nation's actual trade condition, have advanced wonderfully in the last few years. It is to-day fairly well recognized that the commodity trade balance of a nation is neither a true nor yet the best criterion of her condition. Such a trade balance does not take into consideration either the invisible exports or imports or the internal trade of a country. A much truer gauge to-day is the total physical volume and value of a nation's production; but perhaps the most accurate gauge is to be obtained by looking at several phases of national life. The soundness of this contention is easily demonstrated by facts-or perhaps it would be more proper to say, the lack of soundness in the first contention. The United States in 1921, a year of great depression, had a favourable trade balance of approximately $1,900,000,000. In 1923, a year of marked prosperity as compared with 1921, that trade balance had fallen to $376,000,000 or approximately a drop of 80 per cent. If we look at Canada, I believe the same result is demonstrated. Our trade balance this year if it were a true criterion, would indicate a condition of marked prosperity, and yet the statesmen who told our farmers or our merchants, or our manufacturers or our workmen, that we were to-day enjoying great prosperity would be laughed to scorn. Now in following up this subject I wish to take a look at the industrial trend of conditions in the principal
countries of the world, Great Britain, France and the United States, and I think a good point of commencement is to' be found in 1921, the year of that marked depression which gripped every industrial nation of the world from the most southerly to the most northerly, and from that low point we have a gradual improvement during 1922 and 1923 up to the present time.
Turning to the United States, what conditions do we find there? In 1921 the United States felt that depression most severely. There were between three and four million men out of employment. Industrial life in almost every line was at its lowest ebb, and in addition to that, European conditions were bad. The European trade machine was disrupted and unbalanced. In Europe the standard of wages and of living was receding rapidly and unevenly, exchange was fluctuating wildly and currencies were depreciating. In the face of those conditions the United States adopted the policy of protecting her own industrial life and her own trade machine. In May, 1921, she adopted the emergency tariff, and in November of the same year brought in the Fordney tariff. She re-established the activities of her War Finance Corporation to assist her cotton growers, her grain producers and her live stock raisere, and she raised the restrictions on immigration. The trend of industrial life since that time speaks for itself. What do we find happening in the United States? The Department of Commerce reports and the reports of the Federal Reserve Board, which are now very complete and very accurate, show that since 1921 mineral production in the United States has increased by over 40 per cent, industrial production by over 50 per cent; the movement of live stock to primary markets has increased by over 20 per cent; the movement of fruits and vegetables to primary markets has increased by about 25 and 5 per cent respectively. On the other hand, the movement of grain to primary markets has decreased by about 12 per cent-for reasons which I hope to discuss later. The retail trade and the trade of departmental stores in the United States has shown a similar increase and in some lines that increase has been equal to about 50 per cent. Their bank clearings have increased by about $3,500,000,000; their bank deposits have increased by approximately $1,000,000,000, and their bank commercial loans by over $500,000,000. As to ufnemployment, that has practically ceased to exist in the United States, and they are now giving employment to considerable foreign labour, which of course includes Canadian workmen.

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur
In short, without taking up unnecessarily the time of the House, let us say that the United States appears to have adopted adequate remedies, suited to her industrial life, for the protection of her industrial machine against the destructive attack of the unbalanced European trade machine and that her rapid recovery has been the result; and her reward is a most rapid and startling recovery.
Now, let us look at France for a moment. In 1921 France felt severely the same depression, and apparently adopted the same means for the protection of her industrial life. On March 28, 1921 she raised her tariff to possibly the highest point in its history. Owing to the publicity given to the troubles of French government finance, it is perhaps a general feeling that like conditions prevail in private industry and that there conditions are also unfavourable. Such is not the case. If we look at the trade reports of our own commissioner, the trade reports from Washington, and such other trade reports as are available, we find the actual facts. France commenced to recover and she has continued to recover until to-day her iron and steel industries, her coal mines, and her silk, textile and woollen manufactures, her agricultural and her general industrial life, are enjoying a period of very great and very marked prosperity. Her bank clearings have pretty nearly doubled, not quite. Her bank deposits and her commercial loans, which show the activity of business, have increased by about two and a half billion francs each from the end of 1921 to the beginning of 1924. Unemployment in France is unknown. The latest report we have is for January, 1924, and that shows only 596 men unemployed in Paris. Other reports show that France has been importing foreign labour to meet the labour demands within her boundaries. As to the condition of France to-day I do not know of any more complete conclusion than to read the report of our trade commissioner written in January of this year. He says:
To sum up, France's balance sheet for 1923 shows a stabilized budget, reduced expenses, the development of fiscal resources and the extension of foreign trade.
Now, let us look at Great Britain for a few minutes. Great Britain likewise suffered from a very severe depression in 1921. Great Britain adopted certain partial and limited means to protect her industries during that depression, and I am glad to say she has made a certain amount of recovery. She has reduced her unemployment very consider-

ably, but there are still about 1,250,000 men out of work in Great Britain. Her bank clearings between January, 1922 and January, 1924, have increased by about £70,000,000; but her bank deposits and her commercial .bank loans have decreased by about £150,000,000 and £140,000,000 respectively. Her freight-that is the freight carried by her railways-has shown a substantial increase. Her iron and steel industries have advanced, but generally her other industries are considerably below normal. Her industries are, speaking as a general rule, much stronger financially, have much wider trade connections, and greater world banking facilities than the industries of almost any other country but in spite of these advantages, we must admit, from a general view of the trend in England, that the recovery of her industry has been slow, arduous and irregular, and that it is still far from complete. To be fair we must admit that a considerable amount of this has been dbe to strikes and labour troubles; but if we take our own trade commissioner's report we find that his view is even more pessimistic. His report likewise for January, 1924, and his general summary of British trade is that while it is to be hoped that the bottom has been reached, the immediate outlook seems somewhat uncertain. I think, perhaps, he is a trifle too pessimistic. But from the general view of affairs in England we may be certain that she is making a hard struggle; that while her comeback is slow and irregular, we believe the advance she is making is solid and finally she will pull herself through without doubt.
Now let us look at Canada and see if we can get a fairly accurate estimate of our trade condition, of just how we stand in our trade situation. Canada in 1921 suffered the same general depression and it was fairly severe. She, of course, was then under a moderate protective tariff which, while it may have been changed slightly by way of reduction has practically remained the same. We find that in 1921, the net value of Canada's total production was $2,728,000,000 while the net value of her total production for the 3'ear 1922, was about $2,740,000,000, an increase of somewhat under one per cent. The returns for the year 1923, are not yet completed but such returns as are available lead us to believe that we shall enjoy another slight increase. As to her industries, a grouping of her main manufacturing industries and a canvass of their operations show there has been' practically no advance in earnings since 1921-the earnings remain practically

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur
the same. But in certain lines of industry, in our mineral production and in our iron and steel works, advances and recoveries are being made. With regard to our departmental and retail stores it is very difficult to arrive at an accurate conclusion, but so far as we have been able to investigate they are still suffering from considerable depression, and a great many retail stores are barely meeting current expenses. I believe there is plenty of liquid capital in Canada. This was evidenced by the ease and rapidity with which the Dominion loan of $200,000,000 and the Ontario loan of nearly $40,000,000 were absorbed in rapid succession; but the fact remains that so far as industrial development is concerned Canadian capital to-day is more or less frozen. In regard to our railway loadings from points within Canada these have shown a gratifying increase. Our bank clearings have shown between November, 1921, and November, 1923, an increase of about $200,000,000; but our bank deposits have shown a decrease of about $60,000,000, and our bank commercial loans a decrease of about $150,000,000;-I take the corresponding months on account of the seasonal variations which occur in trade. As to unemployment, our number of unemployed since 1921 has materially decreased, but the report for January of this year, the percentage being based upon January of 1920, shows an unemployment in Canada amounting to 7.2 per cent, and that despite the fact of the large number of unemployed who have gone to the United States. Now, much as I should like to report a favourable condition in Canada and a complete recovery and restored prosperity, still, in the face of these facts, and in the face of the fact that our farmers are still despondent, that our workmen are still leaving the country, that our capital is still chary about making any more industrial commitments than are absolutely necessary, we must be frank with ourselves and admit that, while Canada has recovered to some extent, at the same time that recovery has been slow and only partial, and in fact our trade is still below normal.
So far as the trend of conditions in all these four countries is concerned, as well as with regard to the degree of their respective recoveries I think it would serve but little purpose for me to discuss the theory of the situation. The facts, I propose to leave with this House, and I believe they are reasonably accurate and as close to the actual conditions as they can be obtained. I am convinced that anyone who judges these facts with a broad view and without preconceived prejudices, must admit that the tariff policies
of these countries have had at least some influence, and I believe a substantial influence, on the rapidity and the degree of recoveiy ' which has been experienced in them. The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) prefaced his remarks, which explained the proposed tariff changes, by setting forth the trade condition of Canada so far as evidenced by our external business. I believe that was a sound way of approaching a consideration of the tariff changes; but I submit that it should have gone much further and should not only have taken into consideration, or tried to arrive at, the actual trade conditions of Canada, but should have taken into account also the world trend of events, the actual happenings of industrial life in these nations from 1921 to the present time. In my opinion, if (his House will judge the industrial conditions of these countries fairly, and will give a certain weight of consideration to the tariff policies under which their respective returns to prosperity have been brought about, we shall be much more chary of making reductions in the tariff or attempting changes which may impair our industrial life than we ordinarily are.
Let me turn for a few minutes to some of these fiscal changes as proposed by the Acting Minister of Finance. To judge the proposal one must first diagnose the malady, and I think we will all admit that the greatest of our present ills is the one now being experienced by the agricultural industry of Canada. I am going to attempt the perhaps too-ambitious task of analysing that condition, and may venture some suggestions but in doing so, I do not want to be considered as forcing advice upon my friends to the left, and such analysis as I may make is offered not as infallible but as an honest endeavour to arrive at the essentials of the situation. Let me preface my remarks in this connection by saying that I fully appreciate the tremendous importance and the basic nature of our agricultural industry, that I have the fullest sympathy with it, and that I quite realize that its prosperity is of vital importance to Canada as a whole. Now, what are the real causes of our farmers' unfortunate plight? In the first place, we should bear in mind that of all our raw materials, wheat is possibly one of the most internationalized and most subject to foreign conditions. Needless to say, there exists a condition of over-production; and let us remember that wheat is produced but once a year and is subject to weather conditions, so that the farmer cannot as promptly adjust himself to conditions as can
The Budget-Mr. LeSueur

the manufacturer or certain producers of other raw material. We must furthermore keep in mind the fact that, as a general rule, and in the absence of abnormal influences, the curtailment or the increase of the total wheat crop is gradual and extends over a number of years. As to the degree of over-production which exists to-day, the figures given in the Book of International Statistics published at Rome show that during the years between 1909 and 1914 the average world production of wheat, exclusive of Russia, was about three billion bushels, which we may take as a normal figure for normal times. On the other hand, in 1921 and 1922, which were abnormal years, we find that production increased to about 3,116,000,000 and 3,120,000,000 bushels respectively. The biggest consumer of our wheat is Europe, and Europe to-day is below normal, is more or less impoverished. It is estimated that her consumption of wheat and rye, from both domestic and foreign sources, is about 20 per cent below normal. Thus we have a condition in which the supply is above normal and the demand below normal; we have a condition of over-production with all its attendant hardships. But that is only one factor and I believe there exist two other important factors coincident, so far as time is concerned, with this situation and seriously affecting our agriculture. The first of these is a world-wide tendency towards falling prices; and it is a general rule, almost a natural law that just as the price of raw material rises more rapidly than that of the manufactured article, so on the other hand the price of the raw material drops more quickly than that of the manufactured article. This is very well illustrated in the case of wheat, flour and bread. If we look at an imaginary chart, we find that the price of wheat rose in a very irregular line to its peak and that the price of flour followed in a more gradual curve behind the price of wheat until it reached its peak; and then, on the reverse side of the curve, that the fall of wheat came first and in an irregular curve, and flour followed. We find that the price of bread on the other hand followed the course of flour, rose in a jerky line until it reached its peak, and that then it again followed flour in its descent to the normal level. The fact is that, under normal conditions, and without other adverse conditions, the price of wheat would naturally fall to its normal level before the price of the manufactured article would.
In addition, I believe there is another factor which is affecting our western farmer. We have had a most tremendous expansion as [Mr. LeSueur. 3
regards our wheat, both in the acreage sown and in the quantity grown. Under the influence of rising prices and patriotic appeals, our acreage has increased from about 11,000,000 acres in 1913 to about 23,000,000 acres in 1921, 1922 and 1923. It is approximately at that figure to-day. Our wheat 4 p.m. production has increased from about 231,000,000 bushels in 1913 to approximately 470,000,000 last year. Such a tremendous expansion in short periods of time is, in nearly all cases, and has been, I believe, in our case, built largely on credit. The credit granted has been very great and the expansion has been very great. The result is that our western agricultural industry is spread out very thin. This alone is a condition which might prove very hazardous; but when there is added to it simultaneously the condition of .over-production with its attendant hardships and the hardships which attach to a period of falling prices, then we realize to some extent the actual fight which our western farmer has to face and the real problems to be solved. For the agriculturist, struggling as he is in the grip of economic over-expansion and buffeted about by great and inscrutable world forces of over-production and falling world prices, the remedy is proposed of reducing the tariff on agricultural implements, a remedy which, at its most optimistic view, as I understand the matter, can mean nothing more than a saving of ten or fifteen dollars a year to the average farmer, a remedy which carries with it the joker of injuring his home market by possibly destroying or greatly imperilling a great industry, that is taking the budget at its face value, and the remedy proposed is so insignificant and imaginary-if it is a remedy at all, compared with the giant forces from which we are suffering-that it appears trivial and not worthy of consideration. It is like sending a tin fish against the torrent of Niagara.
If we go beyond and do not accept the budget as it stands, but look behind the scene at the new regulation which has recently been issued altering the previous regulation of the dumping clause or special duty, then we find that even that amount of remedy has possibly been removed. The situation as regards the dumping clause is, I believe, clear, and I do not know that any purpose will be served by my going into it. I might, however, just say, in reiterating something which has been said in prior speeches, that for some years past there has been in force a regulation whereby, if the difference between the price paid by the Canadian importer and the price which the same article

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur
has as a fair market value in its place of origin is no greater than 5 per cent, then the dumping duty did not apply. The new regulation, however, issued on April 8, 1924, two days before the budget was delivered, repeals that special clause as to the 5 per cent, and now any machinery or other article coming in would pay full dumping duty. That would mean, as I understand the matter, that if an article is selling in the United States at $100 and the price quoted to the Canadian importer is $95, then under the old system there would be no dumping duty added, but the duty of 10 per cent would be added to that $95 making the price $104.50. Under the present tariff and the new regulation the dumping duty of $5 would be added, and in addition to that a tariff of 6 per cent on the $95, making the price $105.70 to the importer to-day as against the $104.50 before. I am not quarrelling with the protection to our industrial industries; I believe our industrial industries demand an adequate protection; but if the above is the situation, then the government is offering no remedy for our agricultural situation.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Will the
hon. gentleman admit that the removal of that 5 per cent margin in the dumping clause has really had the effect of increasing the incidence of protection all round? I think that was the hon. gentleman's argument and I want to get it clear.
Mr. LeSUEUR: I believe it has increased protection on agricultural implements.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE ACTING MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
In that case would
the hon. gentleman consider that the agricultural implement industry has been hurt at all by these changes?
Mr. LeSUEUR:	I have explained that I
am in favour of the protection of the agricultural implement industry and of all our industries, as I will indicate further on, but I say that under those conditions no remedy is offered either in the budget or in any other action by the government for our western ill.
I will proceed to some suggestions as to our agricultural situation. Are there any real remedies for that ill? Is there anything that we can do to help our agricultural industry in western Canad'a? If the report of the Dawes commission or some other satisfactory solution is adopted in Europe and Europe recovers, then I think we shall have some benefit from that source, but we must remember that Russia will be again entering
the export market, and that the recent agrarian reforms in central Europe are to-day having their effect by way of increased crops, and therefore that we have to face a protracted period in which production will continue to exceed demand.
Under these circumstances, what remedies can we adopt to help our Canadian West? Let me touch first on the foreign market. As I have said, the present situation of overproduction will probably continue for some time. But we have, I believe, a virtual monopoly on one thing and that is on the quality of exported wheat. It is admitted that owing to climatic and soil conditions our wheat contains a larger percentage of gluten than other exported wheats, and therefore it is mixed with soft wheats for maintaining the uniformity and standard of the best flours. Practically all other exported wheats to-day are soft wheats. In Europe it is a well recognized fact that the peculiar quality of our flour is an essential element in the blending necessary for the best standard of flour. In the United States it is also a well recognized fact that this inherent quality is what enables our wheat to jump over any tariff barriers which the United States may erect. Our wheat overcomes the handicap of tariff barriers and finds a firm market in the United States. Now, hardly a bushel of our wheat goes to Central and South America. Those countries to-day have a population of about 90,000,000 people, they can be reached by an all-water route from Vancouver, they are prosperous and can pay for our wheat; they import annually from forty-three to forty-five million bushels of wheat and about twenty million bushels of wheat flour. Their bread is generally of poor quality, and they are anxious to improve it. Therefore I feel satisfied that if we organize and push this business vigourously we can find a market there for at least fifteen million bushels of our wheat every year by reason of its superior quality alone, and a market for at least seven or eight million barrels of our flour, also on the ground of superior quality. The same remark applies more or less to Asia. To-day Asia is importing about thirty-two million bushels of wheat and about seventeen and a half million bushels of wheat flour, of which we are supplying a very small precentage. We have the quality to recommend our wheat and flour, and we should make the most of that weapon supplied by nature in developing a firm and secure market for these commodities. There is no reason why we should not get our trade commissioners in South America busy on this project and so establish a firm and growing

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur
market. It can be done. We might enlist the services of some of our brilliant journalists for the necessary propaganda. And it is generally recognized by industrialists that if you have quality in your goods the marketing of them is only a question of efficient organization. Therefore I would suggest that the development of these new markets be pressed vigorously and sedulously. Let us spend some money for the purpose and forget the completion of the parliament tower for a few years. Of course, we must maintain the quality of our wheat and flour, and I understand that our western provinces are taking steps to this end by encouraging the ' use of good seed and the adoption of crop rotation, and other similar measures.
As to the home market, let us consider what our attitude should be. In the first place, this is a sure market, or at least, it can be made so, for our agricultural industry. It is also our most important market, as can be demonstrated by figures. We find according to the Bureau of Statistics that in 1919 Canada produced 193,260,000 bushels of wheat, of which she exported 78,000,000 bushels and absorbed at home approximately 115,300,000 bushels, or nearly 59 per cent. In this case the home market is first in order and paramount in importance, as it usually is. I feel that any remedy to be a real remedy for our agricultural situation must recognize the fact that the basic unit of our civilization is the nation, must recognize that the integrity of our industrial life must be protected, and the growth of our domestic markets and our internal trade encouraged. In my opinion the present budget does not carry out those conditions. It appears, to say the least, to trifle with the life of the great industries of our country; it appears to extend the black hand of uncertainty toward the throat of a great many of our industrial concerns. That is a most unfortunate and a most unhappy condition, because it stagnates progress and certainly injures our home market.
In connection with our foreign exports especially our exports to South and Central America or other points through Vancouver, I wish to say one or two words on the question of freight rates. I have heard it stated that the regulation of freight rates is an inexact science, and I have no wish to take it out of the hands of those who know something about it. But there is a persistent and constant claim that the rates from Edmonton to Vancouver are out of proportion to the operating costs on that line and out of proportion to the freight rates to the east. As to that, I believe we have a special tribunal which is fitted to investigate, a tribunal which has had experience in railway matters. It has attached to it a body of experts, and there is no reason why the government could not refer the matter to them and get a report setting forth the facts, the decision arrived at and the reasons therefor which might form the basis for any proposed action looking to a change in these conditions. I think that should be done at once; we should get an immediate report on the subject. If these rates can be reduced so that the Edmonton section can get their wheat to Vancouver more cheaply, and thence to the south and other points, it will mean a great relief to

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur
a large section of our western farmers and help all parts of the West.
All these suggestions have more or less the object of helping the farmer to help himself. I believe the farmer has to keep his home market; economically his basic unit should be the nation; our internal trade should be built up and protected. One remedy for some of his difficulties should be found in an energetic propaganda to bring before the southern countries the quality of his wheat, particularly in those sections where the value of the Canadian farmer's product is not known and appreciated, and where the people are looking for and would welcome better wheat, better flour and better bread.
Following out that idea of helping the farmer to help himself, I have always heard since my early days that the farmer was the most independent of men, that he controlled his own livelihood, that his living depended on no other man. If that is not the condition in western Canada to-day, I ask, is there not some feasible scheme whereby it can be made so? Is it not possible to have some co-operation between federal and provincial governments whereby the farmer will be made more or less self-sustaining and thus be able to overcome his present difficulties? Can he not be enabled to produce his own butter, his own eggs, his own meat? It may not be a very high ambition, but it would be sufficient to carry him over the present crisis. My understanding of the situation 'may be wrong, but we do co-operate in road-building and in many other things; why not co-operate in that? Another question that might be asked is this: How far can the government co-operate in enabling some of the western farmers to shift their crop from wheat to some other line?

I would like to ask the hon. member a question-and I appreciate the spirit of his address. Does he take into consideration the great difference between the conditions in the United States, with 110,000,000 consuming people, and those in Canada, with a tremendous producing population and a small consuming public? Does he appreciate how much more difficult the question is to settle in this country?
Mr. LeSUEUR:	I do take that into consideration. I appreciate it and I am trying to offer some solution that will be a step toward relieving that condition. With regard to the present position of agriculture, I would just like to cite the situation which existed in the southern states. It may not be exactly applicable, but it was more or less along the same line. It was about 1830 or 1835, that the cotton producers in the southern states were experiencing a crisis of low prices and overproduction. At that time the Democratic party thought it would be in the interests of that community that they should buy their implements in the cheapest market and sell their cotton abroad, that they should have free trade or low tariffs. A compromise as to tariff was arrived at and the arrangement prevailed for some eight or ten years. Those years were not years of prosperity. War followed in Europe and there was some prosperity, but shortly after that a protective tariff was .adopted in the States and has been followed fairly consistently ever since. To-day the United States is producing about 12,500,000 bales of cotton. Of that amount about
6,000,000 bales are manufactured in the United States, about 4,000,000 of which are manufactured in the southern cotton states. That is just an example which I leave with the House.
In summing up as to this topic, I must admit that I have occupied considerable time and attempted a very ambitious task. I thank the hon. members to my left for their kindly reception of my effort. An analysis of the western situation shows that the condition there is due to this series of causes: *Overproduction, falling prices and over-ex pansion. I believe further if we are going to look for remedy, real and permanent, we have to look directly and hit directly at those causes, and I would like to reiterate, that the very nature of those causes and the very

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur

nature of these remedies must impress upon us that our basic unit must be the nation, that those ills in the West will be best combatted and overcome eventually by the co-operaition and help of our united industrial life, and that the one essential we must keep in mind in our consideration of this subject is the integrity of our complete industrial life. Now let us look for a short time at some of the points in connection with our tariff.

speechtext:
The hon. member has argued that production of wheat should be decreased in the West and that the western farmer should enter mixed farming. Is he of the opinion that the farmers of Ontario and in the East who have largely ceased growing wheat and entered into mixed farming are today in a greater condition of prosperity than the farmers in the West?
Mr. LeSUEUR: I think it 'would be useless to draw a comparison as to degree, as to whether the farmer of the West is in a worse condition than the farmer of the East, but I would say that the whole agricultural situation of our country needs help in every possible way, and that if you help one section you help the other. As to shifting from the growing of wheat to other lines of farming in the West, I do not suggest that that should be done in a wholesale way, but it should be done simply so far as it can be carried out or needs to be carried out to meet the western situation. There should not be an extensive shifting. An extensive shifting would be impossible. It is only as a minor factor I am speaking of it.
Now, turning to a few points in connection with the tariff, let me say that I feel convinced that a great many of our divergencies of opinion are due to differences in our conclusions as to what the facts are, and if we could come more nearly together on what the actual facts are I think our theories would much more nearly coincide. I am firmly convinced that, so far as present world conditions are concerned, an adequate protective tariff is essential to the growth of a diversified industrial life for our country and for the production of that distinct type of manhood which Canada can produce and should have. I do not favour a tariff which allows any manufacturer to make excessive profits; and I believe that the rate of tariff is something which must be determined by the conditions m each particular case, and having regard to the national needs. Now it is almost impossible for any member of this House or for any minister of the government to de-
termine what rate of tariff should prevail in any one particular industry, without being in constant and close touch with that industry both at home and abroad. Half knowledge is, of course, dangerous, and I believe that this country would be wise to have a tariff commission of a scientific nature to advise as to the regulation of tariff needs. Sir Thomas White, as Minister of Finance, in 1912 brought in a bill which proposed to establish a tariff commission, a commission which would have power to investigate and ascertain costs of production, costs of transportation, costs of material, and inquire into any other matters which pertain to industrial concerns, and that the results of their investigations should be available to the House and to the ministers of the Crown. Such a tariff commission would, I believe, in making one investigation after the other, gradually accumulate and tabulate a series' of facts, gather information which would be of vital importance, and would *always prove ,a source of reliable information. If it is true that our differences are to a large extent differences on the facts, and if it is true that suspicions which sometimes arise in the minds of the public are largely due to inability to get at the facts, such a tariff commission would serve a very useful and a beneficial purpose in our national life.

speechtext:
Would the hon. member confine the powers of such a tariff board as he speaks of to the making of investigations and giving advice merely, or would he go beyond that? Would their findings have any further purpose than to advise the government?
Mr. LeSUEUR: That, of course, would be a *matter for much discussion, but what I have suggested so far is only in the nature of an advisory tariff commission, leaving the responsibility with the ministers of the Crown.
There is one other matter in connection with our tariff which I should like to bring up, and that is in connection with our preference. We give to-day a preference to Great Britain. Na person can be more anxious than I am to see our Imperial relations strengthened and grow. The British Empire is to-day a group of free peoples of the same race and the same civilization, and their co-operation and efforts are to-day exercising a very beneficial and a very potent force in the world's advancement. We have a League of Nations, it is true, but I believe that the British Empire is to-day the strongest, the most solid, and the most effective League of Nations which exists in the world, and that in the carrying out of its own interests and its own development it is

The Budget-Mr. LeSueur
advancing the world's best interests. But notwithstanding that, there is no member of this group of free peoples which does not admit the principle that eacji one of its members has the right and the duty to develop its own resources and its own productivity to the utmost without considering the other; that there will be no quarrel between members of the British Empire in seeing each member develop its own production to the uttermost, and that foreign trade only helps in so far as it is subservient to that idea. In short this would mean:	Home trade first;
Imperial trade second; and foreign trade third. As to what the policy of the present government is in this matter I am unable to find out; but let me say this:	Under our present
preferential rates, goods are coming in from Great Britain and are doing serious injury to some of our industrial concerns. If I were asked to give an example of the concerns thus affected I would instance boots and shoes. It is a fact that the agents of several British concerns are visiting various parts of Canada to-day and are selling consignments of boots and shoes to our merchants to the great detriment of our boot and shoe factories. Now, if that injury is due to inefficiency on the part of our boot and shoe manufacturers then the burden must rest on them; but if it is due to differences in cost of production, or differences in wages, or other costs then, I think, our preferential duty should be changed so as to give our manufacturers the proper amount of protection and I doubt very much if the government to-day has the necessary machinery available to determine which of these conditions exist. If so, that is another example where a tariff commission would prove a very efficient and useful body.
Before leaving the question of tariff preferences I might point out that while the home trade should be first, we must not forget that Imperial trade should be second. Thus I view with some regret that the British Chancellor of the Exchequer, in his recent budget, has seen fit to reject the proposals of the Imperial conference and to provide that the McKenna duties which gave the dominions certain preferences should be allowed to lapse. If I understand British politics aright, the policy of the British Labour party has been, and is, more directed to internal and domestic affairs and pays little or no attention to Empire, not, I would say, from a spirit of hostility but from a feeling of more or less indifference to the Empire and this on the ground that the Empire is more or less of a burden and that the principle of Empire is objectionable as implying the oppression of 108jr
free peoples. But, while I feel that their present pronouncement is in greater or lesser degree due to the policy of "buying in the cheapest market," I feel that world conditions are going to force the abandonment of that policy, in whole or in part by the British 'government. I also feel and hope that as the present government in its tenure of office comes more into touch with the dominions, and is brought into more direct contact with the feelings of Imperialism and the desire for a close working Imperial trade arrangement we may see a change in its attitude as disclosed by the recent budget.
There is one other point I propose to discuss and that is with regard to our distribution system, I bring this up because I feel that possibly the government may be able to adopt some remedy in regard to it. We hear complaints about the difference between the price paid to the producer and that paid by the consumer, and to avoid properly studying the matter this situation is blamed on the tariff. I had a striking example of this brought to my attention recently. A farmer had several hogs ready for the market. They weighed about 170 pounds apiece, and the most he could get from the Toronto buyer was eight cents per pound. He went to the local butcher who said he could not buy them because he had a market for only a small portion of the animal. The farmer continued looking round and finally sold them to a butcher on the outskirts of the city and obtained, after losing about 35 pounds of weight in dressing the hogs, sixteen cents a pound. By selling the hog locally, instead of to the Toronto buyer he made a gain of $8 per hog. That situation is not, I think, the fault of the central butcher, or of the consumer, or of the producer. The fact is that when the hog is sent to Toronto the meat is cut, trimmed and otherwise decorated. It is then returned in nice shape to the central butcher. The position is that the freight must be paid from the point of sale to the city, then there is the cost of the extra trimming and decorating which the abattoir company makes, and fianlly the cost of freight back. This system has been an insidious growth. I do not know of any one particular branch which is to blame, but this system has grown to such a size that no particular man or group of men can cope with it. However, I believe that a system which is now being used in the United States could be considered by us -with profit. They have there what they call the Department of Simplified Practice. The business of that department is to co-

have listened with a great deal of interest to the speech of the hon. member for West Lambton (Mr. LeSueur), and while I think that we can agree with him in regard to some of the views he has expressed, I do not think that he 'has given us an adequate explanation of the difficulties under which agriculture is labouring at the present time. The fact is that there are a great many causes to which the present situation may be attributed, one of which I think is the fact that the relative prices of things are so .uneven; t'he prices of the products the farmer has to sell are not commensurate with the prices of the things he has to purchase. The two are not compatible. Now, the question that we have to solve is, how we shall alleviate this depression in agriculture. In the United States they proposed to remedy the situation by a different means from the one we have adopted in the present budget; they decided upon protection. The farmers of the United States deemed if wise to have protection because they thought it would solve their problem for them. But the fact is that you will find in the United States to-day that the problem has not been solved and the farmers there are in as difficult a position as they were in before they passed their- high tariff protecting their agricultural products from the competition of the world. You will find in New York state, in Minnesota and in other states, that the farmhouses are boarded up just as they are in different parts of Canada. I regret to say that in our own part of the Dominion that condition prevails, and hundreds of farmers have been going to the United States. That is also the case throughout other parts of Canada, and it is due to some condition that is very hard to diagnose. The government has attempted in this way to grant some relief, and I think it is wise to make the attempt at least by reducing the tariff and abolishing the sales tax. The tariff affects our dairying, poultry raising and all the other different branches of farming. [DOT] It is a wise experiment at any rate, to make this reduction in order to see if it will help the farmers in the business which they are pursuing.
The Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb), in his resolutions, proposes first to extend the British preference to some territories that are under the League of Nations and also to withdraw the preference from some others. I am not going into the particulars of that. His next resolution deals with tea, which will affect households in every part of the country, perhaps in a very small way, but this is a move in the direction of helping households to get through more economically. Other industries that are affected are the fruit growing industry, the poultry industry, the dairy industry. These are industries that we in the East have a good deal to do with, and let us hope that the reductions will be of assistance. I should like to see a little more sportsmanship on the part of those who talk of protection being increased for the benefit of the manufacturers. They realize that the farmers are in this position throughout Canada, and yet I would suggest that they be sportsmen enough to have a unity of feeling with them to help them to get out of that position. It is in the interest of the manufacturers that the farmers should progress, because the farmer cannot buy unless he is able to sell his product at a profit. He cannot let the cream of his work go away to others continually. I am reminded of a little story that I might tell illustrating the struggle that the farmer has. It is an old fable about two frogs going out one morning and falling into a large pan of cream. They struggled for some time and at last one fellow looked at the nature of the liquid and as he could not understand it, he gave up the struggle and dropped to the bottom. The other frog kept struggling along and after a while he found a little lump. He kicked and kicked still more, struggling to get out of that dish, and at last a lump of butter appeared, so he stood on the lump of butter, sprang out, and his life was saved. We need a little of that cream reserved for the farmers so that their lives may be saved. If the cream is going to be taken away from them by the railway freight rates, tariffs and taxes, they cannot make much headway and we want them to succeed.
I wish to refer to the amendment moved by the leader of the Labour party (Mr. Woodsworth). I am in favour of one part of it, that is in regard to the inheritance duty. I think it is the most equitable system of adding to the revenue that the government can adopt, and my reason for saying so is this-and I have studied the philosophy of the matter-that when people accumulate large estates and do so under the legislation that we pass here, it is right, when they pass away, that the country where this money has been earned should in some way receive com-

Well, you would find our sea trout unexcelled. We would like to have some of you make a visit to the island during the summer in order that you may enjoy a healthy dip into the breakers on the north shore. It is a country that will go ahead; the production was better last year than it had ever been, but what is missing is an adequate price for our products. Our position is something like that of the West, where there was a very large yield but not enough realized because the price was wrong and freight- rates were too high. We are in the same fix. It is not the fault of the present government, mind you. It was under the former government that the freight rates were made so high; it was under the former government that the Crowsnest pass agreement was changed and the rates put up. You remember how we were criticized in respect to the Crowsnest pass agreement the year before last; we four members from Prince Edward Island were denounced for voting for the legislation then introduced. But what has

The Budget-Mr. Mackinnon
happened? The return to the Canadian Pacific since the restoration of the old agreement has been better than if was during the period when the suspension was continued. It is well that we should have these facts in mind, because we have been accused of losing to the Maritime provinces $17,000,000 by our vote in favour of the restoration of the Crowsnest pass agreement. Men like Mr. Beatty and Mr. Hanna predicted that they would lose millions by the change, but it turned out the very opposite; their judgment did not happen to be right.
I have referred to this matter of freight rates because it affects us a great deal. We pressed very hard to get the freight rates reduced, because our people were carrying their goods with horses owing to the fact that they could not afford to ship by rail. The railway returns in the Maritime provinces have not been good, simply because the people are .too independent to ship by rail when they have to pay such high freight rates. The new board made some reductions very soon after their appointment, and the situation improved accordingly. But we cannot hope to have the country prosper unless our workshops are kept going and unless we have easy and cheap means of conveyance from one place to the other both for goods and for people; I think that goes without saying. These are the greatest drawbacks that affect us down there. Special rates for tourists would be appreciated.
I wish the Minister of Railways (Mr. Graham) were here. I had intended to bring a matter to his attention, but perhaps the Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) will do it for me. We have a good many people leaving our province. It is proposed to spend a considerable sum for immigration. There were two little branch railroads proposed and agreed to both by Liberals and Conservatives in this House as far back as 1911, the New London and Rustico branches. Plans were prepared and sites allotted for buildings and so on, but the work was never gone on with. In New London we have people whose fathers or grandfathers came from Scotland a hundred years ago, and in Rustico we have the descendants of French Acadian settlers. It is two hundred years since the first settler went into the Rustico district. What I ask the Minister of Railways, through the Minister of Justice, is that while he is providing for the settlers in the new districts in the West by twenty-six branch line resolutions he should not forget the descendants of the old settlers in the districts I mention, who have been there for 100 and 200 hundred years. Let him give us these branch lines this coming summer so that

we may have a celebration and the return of our own people.
Yesterday a man well known in public life who came from Prince Edward Island passed away in the person of the late Chief Justice of Canada, Sir Louis Davies. He was highly honoured in the province and in Canada as a whole; his career was long and honourable and an inspiration to the young men of the province. Undoubtedly his field was larger than it would have been had he remained in the province and practised law, but his illustrious career is only one instance. Go to another room in this building and you will find Sir Robert Falconer and the Reverend Doctor Pringle who came from Prince Edward Island, fighting on one side of the church union question, and on the other side the Reverend Doctor Fraser and one or two others. Doctor Pidgeon is a descendant of the Pidgeons of New London, Prince Edward Island. I mention these simply as instances of men now in the struggle who came from the province by the sea. Had they remained down there they probably would have worked at farming or something of that kind, but their education was good and they have gone out to other parts of the continent. You find them from California to Massachusetts and all through our western country-workmen, clergymen, doctors, lawyers and judges. I could give you the names of many who have gone out and have attained eminence in different parts of the world. I will mention just two others, if you will permit me; one is J. Gould Schurman, who grew up on a farm in Prince Edward Island, was president of a university in the United States and to-day is ambassador for the United States in China. Another was Franklin K. Lane, who was a distinguished member of the cabinet of President Wilson during the war.
I do not mention these things in a spirit of boasting; I am simply pointing out that although the place is small it is turning out .men who have proved their worth in other parts.
We have fewer people there by ten thousand than we had when we entered confederation, but we are not inclined to secession; we believe in standing by the union; we believe in Canada going ahead. But we cannot get population without industries. There is a splendid opening for industry in Prince Edward Island if the capitalists would, instead of concentrating their activities in large centres, establish branch houses in other parts of the Dominion. I admit that the practice of concentrating in the large centres

The Budget-Mr. McConica
is good from the point of view of foreign trade, but it is ruinous for our local industries. Many of our sons have gone out to the world, so that part of the intellectual force of the island has been spent in other provinces and countries, and although we do not have the benefit of it, I think it is well spent and that we have no reason to regret it.
Mr. T. H. MeCONICA (Battleford):	Mr. Speaker, I have no disposition to prolong this discussion, but there are a few observations that I should like to make. To my mind this budget and the amendment offered by the hon. member for Kent (Mr. Doucet) raise a very important issue in Canada today, the question whether the future fiscal policy of Canada is to be a tariff for protection or a tariff for revenue.	That, it
seems to me, is the issue. That is where we stand to-day as a parliament and as a country. Now, for my part, if that issue is fairly joined, I would take my position in favour of a tariff for revenue. We have had a good deal of talk about free traders, but there is no use discussing this question except as it stands. I do not think any one in this House to-day is in favour of putting this country under free trade at any time in the near future. We believe in a revenue tariff, with such incidental protection as that affords.
Now what is a protective tariff? It is a tax levied for the purpose of protection. It is levied for the purpose of taxing the many to protect the few. It taxes the money out of the pocket of one private individual into the pocket of another private individual, and I do not think that is the proper function of government. I deny that a government has the moral right to say to one man: I will 'help you, and I will do so by hurting your neighbour. That is what protection is when you reduce it to its final essence. Now what excuse is there for this proceeding? What good end is obtained by this discrimination between our citizens, for that is what it is? It is taking from one and giving to another, for what purpose? Why, the hon. gentleman says, we will be able to build up the home market; that is the great desideratum. Well, in the first place, can we do it? In the second place, what does it amount to if we can do it? So long as the price is the same, I cannot see that it makes any difference to the man who sells whether he sells in the home market or abroad. There may be some sentimental reason why he would prefer to sell at home; perhaps he would like to bring in people to associate
with him and to whom he could sell, but so far as the money that goes into his pocket is concerned, I cannot see that there is any difference between the home market and the foreign market. So far as bringing relief, for instance, to t'he wheat grower of the West is concerned, there is no difference.
Take our wheat. Our price is fixed in Liverpool, and the Canadian consumer pays the Liverpool price, less the cost of sending the wheat to Liverpool. The producer in western Canada realizes exactly the same price in both cases, and it makes no difference to him financially whether the wheat stops in Ontario or goes on across the water. So as far as relief is concerned, the home market is not of any particular consequence. Suppose we bring people in here. Well, the price of our wheat is fixed by the world price, and if we could transport enough people to Canada to eat our wheat, they would not eat any more wheat here than they would if we left them in Europe, would they? Not a bit; perhaps not quite as much, for there I understand the ration is a bowl of soup and a loaf of bread, while over here we have meat and potatoes, vegetables and fruit and everything else, so I think they would eat rather more wheat on the other side of the water. So far as a market is concerned, this home market is a myth.
Another thing: We are raising about 300,000,000 bushels more wheat than we consume. We raised last year 470,000,000 bushels, and we eat about 50,000,000 bushels or a little less than that. A man eats between five and six bushels of wheat a year, or about
50,000,000 bushels for eight and a half million people. We also sow about 50,000,000 bushels a year, or a little less than that. We have at least 300,000,000 bushels of wheat to ship abroad. Now suppose we tried to consume that wheat at home; 300,000,000 bushels divided by six means 50,000,000 people to bring in here to consume that wheat, and not one of them would be raising wheat. What would they do? That is the question. If we build up this home market they talk about, what are we going to do with these 50,000,000 people? Are they going to manufacture? Where will they sell their stuff? The hon. gentleman says that we should be self-contained; we should live on what we produce. Now we can produce enough to keep ourselves and still have a large surplus. What are we going to do with it? Send it abroad? We are self-contained, we are raising what we need and we should send our stuff abroad; load a shipload of our products, send it to the markets of the world and

The Budget-Mr. McConica
sell it, and bring back a shipload of money; then load another ship and bring back another shipload of money. But how long could we keep that up? We would not get three cargoes out of this country till they would say:	We
will buy your stuff if you will b.uy ours; our money is all gone. Yes, Mr. Speaker, we must depend for our foreign trade on our ability to buy foreign goods. There is no other way of doing business, and we cannot build up a foreign market unless we buy abroad. Fifty millions of people brought into Canada and engaged in manufacturing or any other vocation you could put them at would not eat a bit more wheat than if they had stayed in Europe. We would not have a market for an additional bushel.
The hon. gentleman says we are producing too much wheat. Well, they are buying all we send to them; they take all we produce. He also says the price is too low. But the price is not going down; it is as good this year as it was last. That is not saying much for it, but that is the situation. He also offers very good suggestions as to how we can relieve our farmers. They should not produce so much wheat, he says, and they should sell at a better price. But how are you going to get a better price? Then he says we must go into other lines of farming. Now what other line, I would like to know? I am a farmer and I am ready to shift to some other line. I have shifted to other lines, and it does not pay. There is nothing else that can be suggested for a farmer in the West to engage in. Talk about the dairy business-we cannot compete writh eastern Canada in that. Why Our cows are practically all dry fed for ten months in the year. We have a little fresh grass for feeding purposes along about the beginning of June, and then it dries up and our cows are practically fed on hay for the balance of the year; they give scarcely any milk. We cannot manufacture dairy products and compete with the farmers of Ontario and Quebec, even if we were as close to the market as they are. We are told to go into some other line, go in for raising cattle. I have raised cattle; I am raising cattle now. It takes ten acres of our prairie grass to keep a steer. That ten acres will cost $200. At 8 per cent that is $16 a year. You can summer the steer on that ten acres but then you have got to winter him. Sixteen dollars a year for three years. That is $48 and you will do mighty well if you can sell him for $30. That is the cattle business. We are told to go into some other line. I want to say to you that the other lines are worse than wheat, and I have tried 
a good many of them. We are told that the aggregate reduction in the price of agricultural implements is not going to help us much. The reduction will not help us a whole lot, but it will help some. The hon. gentleman to my right (Sir Henry Drayton) told us that we would only save about $750,000 by this tariff reduction on agricultural implements.

speechtext:
Well, it is not so much the revenue, it is the bounty we pay to the manufacturer. Then the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) said " Why the farmers of the West need not complain about their agricultural implements because the member for Brandon (Mr. Forke) says they are not buying any implements." That is true, they are not buying implements to any great extent. They are, Mr. Speaker, using old worn out implements, and there is not much economy in it. It is the worst waste they can be guilty of to drive a poor seeder across a field and probably lose two or three bushels per acre when if they had a good machine it would pay for itself in a single year. It is the same with a binder that does not work well. If you had an efficient machine you would soon make up the cost. The reason the farmers are using old machinery is not because they are economical but because they have not the money to buy the new machinery which they need. The farmers of the West have got to the position where they have to save every dollar, or not spend money that should be spent, in order to make their operations profitable.
Hon. gentlemen to our right have told us that the tariff is the great panacea. They *ay ' Take the United States. It has become rich and opulent because it has a protective policy." Well, as another hon. member very truly said, the United States has become rich and opulent in spite of its protective tariff. The republic to the south is in a very different situation to Canada. The United States is practically a world by itself. It is a self-contained nation. It has a diversity of products and climate. It produces practically all it consumes, and consumes practically all that it produces. Its foreign trade does not amount to anything to speak of-that is from a percentage basis.
The states of the Union trade among themselves. The cotton raiser sells to the north, and buys from the north, and so it is. Over there they supply their own wants, manufacture for their own industrial needs, and

The Budget-Mr. McConica
their exportation of commodities is very little. I have here a statement from the United States Minister of Commerce, the Hon. Herbert Hoover, in an article entitled "Economic prospects of 1924" in which he says: "Less than 6 per cent of our total production is exported." Loss than 6 per cent! It is a free trade nation, a nation that trades with itself. There are no trade barriers in the United States. He also says "Less than one per cent of our manufactured products find a market in Europe." So it is a great free trade country. Thirty-five or forty years ago the manufacturing was done in the New England states. They had a tariff' but no internal tariffs. The factories were old and well established, and well financed and managed. They were located in Massachusetts, Connecticut and the eastern states. They had all the advantage of mass production and everything. They had, according to the theory - of our protectionist friends, the best of the situation down there. Take Fall River, Massachusetts. It was the centre of the cotton manufacturing industry. They had great mills there that were supplying the world's market. They controlled that market. They thought their climate was the only climate in the United States where cotton could be manufactured-just the right amount of humidity they told us and just the right temperature, and so the only place where cotton could be manufactured. What happened? They started to manufacture cotton down in. the southern states. Free trade! Why in New England they thought they were right in the position to kill out those fellows who started down there. According to the theory of the protectionist they could just crush them like an egg shell. To-day, as an hon. member stated here, four million out of the six million bales produced are manufactured down below Mason and Dixon's line.
What is true of the cotton business is true of every other line of manufacturing in the United States. The great manufacturing establishments of the United States are in the West, not in New England. They have been started and built up in the central and western states where there are great hives of industry. That is where you find the manufacturing trade of the United States, and it has all grown up in the last thirty-five years under free trade conditions. Now, if they can do that over there why can they not do it in Canada? They tell us that fortunes have been made down there. It is true. Probably the most successful manufacturing establishment in the United States is the Standard Oil Company. I apprehend it is probably the most successful enterprise
the world has ever seen. It took a comparatively unimportant product, a hatural product, a product that is found the world over

Do not forget
Ford and the tin Lizzie.
Mr. MeOONICA: -and they manufactured that into a commodity that is used generally,, for which there is a universal demand. They work that product up into a hundred different commodities to-day; it is the most closely manufactured article in the history of the world. That company have paid good wages and have never had a wage strike in their entire existence. Still they have competition. There are hundreds of other refiners and thousands of independent producers, and yet they have built up fortunes fabulous in amount. Their directors are founding colleges, financing great enterprises, and establishing hospitals. It is a wonderful business which has never had a single farthing of protection, and what it has done other companies can do. It has stood firmly on its own feet and has done business with the whole world. It has met universal competition and ias held its place in the trade of the world, so that its products are to be found wherever there are people to buy them. I repeat, this great enterprise has grown up without the slightest protection. -Now, why cannot Canada do the same? Here we are with boundless natural resources, with our own food supply at home, and with the cheapest and best power in the world. We have a great inland system of waterways that gives us access to the markets of the world at cheap rates, and we have a class of workmen as intelligent, as industrious, and as efficient as can be found anywhere. Yet we cannot compete at home, we cannot compete abroad, we cannot compete anywhere. After fifty years of coddling, and nursing and boosting, our manufacturing enterprise is so frail and wobbly that it is crushed with a shadow. That is the situation. Why, an hon. member yesterday told us that the agricultural implement business was ruined entirely; whereas before a $100 implement was fisted at $95, paid $9.50 tariff and was sold for $104.50, to-day, under our present arrangement, it was going to be listed at $100, with a tariff of $6 and would sell for $106. Our implement dealers, he said, could not stand the competition and were going to be ruined. Imagine, $1.50 of a rise in price and it spells ruination to our home industry. That sort of competition means their destruction, their annihilation. I do not understand the logic of it; at least that logic is a little involved.

The Budget-Mr. McConica
I am not in favour of the proposed amendment (Mr. Woodsworth). There are some things in it that I like, but as I understand the proposition, it seems that we are to condemn the government or at least to vote a want of confidence in them. Now, we are not trying to improve their budget with the amendment. If this amendment were carried it would not change the budget but would simply be a vote of lack of confidence in the administration. That is all it would be. And having voted for the amendment declaring a want of confidence in t'he government, ten minutes later we would vote for the budget and so sustaining the government that we had no confidence in! I do not want to put myself in that position; I do not believe that it is a position which we ought to assume as a party over here. I should have preferred to have seen a square issue between the proffered amendment of the hon. member for Kent, N.B. (Mr. Doucet), and the budget as it has been brought down.
I congratulate the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) upon his budget speech and upon the underlying principle of it. I accept the statement that has been made, that the question is as between low tariff and high tariff, and I am for the low tariff. The fight is on, and I say to my hon. friends to my right, "We will meet you at the next election on that issue and will trim you."
