[The letters handed in are as follows:
The Brown Boggs Co., Limited
The writer feels certain that you are well aware of what a misfortune it would be to Canada if this proposed legislation goes into effect. While most of the changes do not effect this company directly, indirectly it will have a very serious effect, when you consider the large number of manufacturers of agriculture implements and saw mill and mining machinery operating in this ^country.
These people are among our customers, and we probably sell 25 per cent of our product to them. If they are working under a handicap, and their business shrinks, it is only reasonable that' our trade with them will be cut off, as no company will purchase new equipment unless they are expanding or prospering. This will also react of necessity on other manufacturers
from whom we purchase our raw materials, as our volume of business will be lessened.
The working-man will also feel the effect of this curtailing of production, and necessarily the merchants from whom they buy.
We will suffer from U.S. competition as some of the largest manufacturers in this country are branch concerns, and will be able to import considerable of their products from the parent factory in the United States where they can manufacture certain lines more cheaply than in Canada, owing to the greater production.
The preferential tariff on English goods interferes with us directly to quite an extent as it allows goods made in England under a much lower wage rate than we must pay, to come into Canada and under-sell us.
Then, as you are aware, Germany is making great efforts to get a foot-hold in this country, and is advertising very extensively here now. When one considers the difference between what the German workman can live on and what the Canadian workman has a right to receive, it is not hard to understand how they can ship goods in here and sell them at less than our actual cost.
The "Dumping clause" which was put into force some years ago had a good effect at one time, but the writer doubts very much if it has been enforced recently.
Yours very truly,
The Brown Boggs Co., Ltd.
April 24, 1924.
The Ford-Smith Machine Company Dear Sir:-
We wish to draw your attention to the anxiety with which we view the proposed tariff changes now before the House. We are not manufacturers of agricultural implements, and we are not directly affected, as far as we can see at the present time, by these proposed changes, but we are indirectly very greatly affected, and view these changes with great alarm.
This company designs and manufactures machinery, dies, jigs and fixtures which are used by other metal working plants, including implement manufacturers, and anything that affects them, naturally has its consequent effect on us, and our employees.
This company located in Canada well aware of the disadvantages of a small market, and with a full knowledge of the growth of the machinery business in United States under their protective tariff. Had we ever thought that it might be that this tariff would be reduced materially, we would have considered it business suicide to locate a business of our nature in this country, and we would not have done so.
If the present tariff changes go into effect, though it is difficult for us to estimate our loss of sales and employees, because there are many other industries whom we serve and who themselves will also be indirectly affected, we would say that this legislation might depress our sales from 25 to 40 per cent, causing us to lay off skilled mechanics to this extent.
You no doubt have heard in a general way about our mechanics leaving for the other side, but if you were in touch with the situation as we are here, you would get a shock that would surprise you. I am sure that this condition is not properly appreciated in Ottawa. The present position is that we are training young men as apprentices in our technical schools built at tremendous public expense, for the benefit of the United States manufacturer. It is not idle talk, but is the plain statement of facts, that the opportunity for a skilled man to-day is across the line. Our largest competitor is of course the United States manufacturer. It is only by the most strenuous efforts that we are able to compete even at the present time, and if the present advantage of the tariff is

1710	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Hamilton)
reduced, it is very problematical whether such people as ourselves can stay in business in this country.
We cannot impress upon you too strongly the seriousness of the present situation, and we would repeat in conclusion that if this country has to be a manufacturing as well as an agricultural country, that we shall have to have a proper measure of protection till such times as our Canadian quantities are large enough to allow us to specialise in the same way as our foreign competitors; and we would again point out that the strong home competition will insure the proper prices to our consumers.
Yours truly,
The Ford-Smith Machine Co., Ltd.
April 21, 1924.
The International Harvester Company
F. M. Morton, general superintendent of the International Harvester Company of Canada. Limited, Hamilton branch, issued the following statement, regarding the situation arising from the new budget tariff.
" The situation produced by the new budget tariff is a matter of grave concern to the International Harvester Company of Canada, Limited. We do not see how the lowered duties can fail to have a serious and prejudicial effect upon the companj''s manufacturing operations at Hamilton and Chatham. How serious only the future can tell. All we can say is that the company will do its best to meet the situation and keep its plants in operation so long as tariff laws and business conditions will permit. This will be done not only to protect the investment of the stockholders, but the means of livelihood of its employees and their home investments made in the belief that Hamilton and Chatham would continue as prosperous manufacturing communities, assured of encouragement by the country at large.
In the same way as the prosperity of these communities is bound up with that of the industries located in their midst, so in a larger sense the prosperity of the farmers of Canada is also affected. They cannot profit in the long run by making unprofitable the industries which have heretofore supplied their needs. The future of Canada must depend on the mutual prosperity of agriculture and industry, just as in the United States the prosperity of the country has been dependent on the prosperity of these two activities.
We hope the farming communities will come to recognize this relationship and insist on fair treatment to industry, not only as a matter of justice to the investors and great number of their fellow-citizens employed as workmen therein, but for their own enlightened self-interest.
International Harvester Co. op Canada Limited. April 17, 1924.
Dominion Sheet Metal Corporation, Limited
For the past several years our main competition has been against the United States producers, where a duty of 12 1/2 per cent is somewhat assisted by average United States exchange rate of one to three per cent.
Now, however, the import competition has swung around almost entirely to the British sheets with their low labour cost, and the 7 1/2 per cent duty on galvanized sheets from United Kingdom is entirely wiped out by the present depreciated English currency, being about 10 per cent or more below the Canadian par.
You will thus see that the man who buys galvanized sheets can take the money with which he would pay us and can pay the 7 1/2 per cent duty and have 2 1/2 or 3 per cent left over when buying the English sheets.

We are the only concern doing, this work in Canada, and have had a very difficult time for several years but finally have the industry pretty well established, but it is only on account of an efficient organization and low overhead cost that we are able to compete at all and that in a restricted district.
We sincerely hope that something will be done in the way of adding a certain amount, based upon the per cent of depreciation, this amount to be added to the duty, as it seems only fair to us that this duty being figured on a normal value of currency from the exporting countries should be increased when their currency becomes depreciated; otherwise the original intent of the duty is not being carried out.
We and our entire staff and force of employees, together with co-operation industries furnishing us with raw materials here "would certainly appreciate some release from this situation. [DOT]
Yours very truly,
Dominion Sheet Metal Corporation, Limited. April 17, 1924.
Collins, Never-Fail Products, Limited
We are producers of a line of poultry raising supplies including incubators and brooders, as well as a line of spraying equipment for use by horticulturists.
In view' of the new' changes in the tariff we have decided to suspend the manufacture of brooders and incubators as well as the sprayers with one -or two small exceptions, and to import these and job them.
This will cut our expense down because we will dispense not only with a considerable number of workmen but some of the office staff as w'ell, and the small jobbing profit will be one we can depend upon rather than take a chance on a larger manufacturing profit.
Might say for your information that last year under the old tariff we came within a few dollars of breaking even, sustaining a slight loss on the manufacturing of the incubators and brooders and the spraying equipment, and this year wre w'ere hoping for an increase in the demand and an opportunity to make a profit, but' in view' of the change we have decided to suspend manufacturing and go into jobbing, selling U.S. lines, which we are able to import now at less than we can manufacture.
This comprises about half our manufacturing operations and we pay out from twelve to fifteen thousand dollars a year in labour, and four or five thousand dollars a year in clerical and staff payroll, and this will be cut in two.
The worst feature in our estimation is the fact that instead of progressing and growing we will now' be entirely obliterated as far as the Canadian industry is concerned, and we are quite sure that if we cannot manufacture at a profit no one else can in Canada.
Yours very truly,
Collins, Never-Fail Products. Limited.
April 17, 1924.
P. B. Yates Machine Company Limited
We are greatly concerned and apprehensive as to the general effect tariff reduction is having and will have on business at large in Canada. .
As a result of the war, a greater number of diversified commodities have been produced and can be obtained in the Dominion, with the result that 99 per cent of our purchases have been made in the home markets, and 90 per cent right here in Hamilton, a thing not possible prewnr.
With assurance, under a stabilized tariff, have been able to measure the future w'ith some degree of confidence, resulting in investment of our money in materials and labour, in other words, building up stock against future prospects, thus creating markets
MAY 2, 1924	mi
The Budget-Mr. Stewart (Hamilton)
for materials and keeping labour employed over low business areas.
To meet conditions which the lowering of the tariff and increase in British preference has brought about, we must seek the lower or cheaper foreign markets that are thrown open to us to the exclusion of our home markets; if that situation exists with us it also affects hundreds of others. That is the condition we are apprehensive ol, we live with and upon each other, -what affects one affects all.
There was such a reversal of business in our line, during the interval the Speech from the Throne to the time the budget was brought down, as to result in a complete change in our producing policy.
There is not that confidence in the future facing us as to warrant our taking the financial risk in accumulating material and keeping labour employed, only as can be applied to actual orders in hand, resulting in our having to lay off a number of men and curtail hours of employment, of the balance, to 30 hours per week, and material purchases.
This not only adds to the unemployed, it means the loss of our and their purchasing power, further loss to the city of Hamilton and to the Dominion.
From a beginning in 1907 to a business in 1911-12-13 giving employment to 380 under the stabilized tariff of the Laurier government to a dwindling to 96 employees under a shifting tariff of the King government, the like of which we have not had in our career of 17 years.	*
The increase in British preference has thrown open to English competition a market for machines, under Item No. 453-B, that they have heretofore not been able to enter, competition in respect of wages paid, hours worked and cost of materials we have little hope of meeting. We know what this competition is, as we have learned from our losses in Australia, and competition which Australian manufacturers are complaining seriously of to their own government.
The attention of the government has been called to the fact that Canada alone has seen fit to reduce her tariff, the results of which are fast becoming apparent in comnarisnn to ftp '[DOT]ov.ntry tc the south us, wiLh its protective wall against us and our western contemporary, "the Farmer", in particular.
On the one hand our government is spending money to increase immigration, while that to the south is spending money to keep it out, except our own favored artisans and mechanics, no quota is placed against them; there is, however, a tariff,
Item-Homan beings, $8.00 per head.
Money will go where business is to be had, and employment and immigration will follow; every restriction, every obstacle placed in its way will cause it to flow in the opposite direction, and those obstacles are now placed with the adoption of this budget which are going to be felt, not by the individual, not by a faction, not by a section, but by all the people and our country as a whole.
Yours truly,
P. B. Yates Machine Co. Ltd.
April 24, 1924.
Imperial Cotton Company Limited
April 19th, 1924.
On the basis of our sales to the agricultural implement manufacturers during 1923, our future annual sales will be reduced over ten per cent and our yearly production will be decreased approximately twelve per cent; which, in terms of our personnel, would affect about thirty-five employees, whose earnings aggregate over $30,000 per annum.
By the terms of the proposed reduction of tariff on materials supplied the agricultural implement manufacturing industry , our protection as against the United States will be cut twelve and one-half per
im	'
cent, whereas England will now have a preference over us, on the present rate of exchange, of at least three per cent in the Canadian market; and other countries with depreciated exchange will have an opportunity afforded them to offer severe competition.
Under the present method of assessing duty on depreciated exchange from foreign countries, it is now a hardship to compete with the protection afforded us by the present tariff and, in many instances, we are obliged to accept business at a distinct loss in order to hold the trade which we have endeavored to build up over a period of nearly twenty-five years.

April 19, 1924.
Bird & Son Limited
Owing to the restricted purchasing power of our customers which has shown itself during the past few months, and particularly during the past one or two months, we have been forced to reduce the number of employees to a lower point than at any time during the past six to eight years. An investigation leaves no doubt in our minds that the cause is nothing else except a lack of confidence in the fiscal Policy of the present government.
While our business is not directly affected by the proposed tariff reductions in the budget recently handed down, nevertheless it is already apparent that these reductions will reduce the number of customers by emigration from Canada to the United States, and that the earning and spending power of those cus-tcrr.crG	i cumin in Canada will be materially
reduced.
Based upon the present outlook therefore, we can only anticipate lower production in our plants and consequently- higher costs, all of which will place United States manufacturers of our lines in a stronger position to take a larger share of the business which would otherwise come to our own plants and other plants similar to our own in Canada.
The employees of our plants both here and in Quebec are consumers of the farm products of the surrounding districts, and it is not only probable, but almost certain that as the purchasing power of our employees decreases, the sales of the farmers in the surrounding district will proportionately decrease.
Yours very truly,
Bird & Son Limited.
April 25, 1924.
Stanley Steel Company Limited
We are drawing to your attention the charges in tariff as brought down by the recent budget, and how it will affect our business.
We- have been manufacturing cold rolled steel for * implement manufacturers for some years. This change in the tariff means that not only do we lose the tonnage that we have been selling the implement manufacturers, but the labour that they are employing in manufacturing parts from the steel we sold them, will be gone, as it is now cheaper for them to bring these parts in from the States in a manufactured condition, the tariff arranging for their entry on the free list.
Our production will be considerably affected by this change, and if similar changes are on the programme,
1712	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Stewart {Hamilton)
it means that the number of our employees will be decreased.
We also wish to point out that on cold rolled steel being imported into this country for export work, there is a draw-back on this material of 99 per cent. We are forced to pay the government, on 12 gauge and heavier (hot rolled steel) that we import to cold roll in Hamilton, a duty of $7 per ton. This duty which we pay, is again paid out by the government to concerns who are bringing in their cold rolled steel from the States on a 99 per cent drawback basis.
You will agree with us that this is not a fair condition. It is a hardship imposed on Canadian manufacturers who have started plants in Canada, since these items were put on a draw-back basis by the government. If we are to employ labour, pay taxes to the government, and build up this country, is it not possible to get some relief, to allow us to increase the number of employees on our pay-roll, and be in a position to pay them wages which will ensure their staying in the Dominion of Canada?
Yours very truly,
Stanley Steel Company Limited.
April 17, 1924.
National Steel Car Corporation, Limited
I might draw to your attention the fact that tariff item No. 453-B, among other things, includes logging cars, the general tariff on which has been decreased from 30 per cent to 20 per cent.
The writer happens to be president also of a car company in the United States, who are probably the biggest logging car producers in that country, and whose patents are based on steel constructed logging railroad equipment. Steps have been taken to give this National Car Corporation here in Hamilton the use of these patents and construction details, and the writer recently returned from the Pacific coast where he looked over the logging operations in that section of the country.
Of course, this action of lowering the tariff is much more detrimental to the development of Canadian industry, and particularly Hamilton, than it is to the investors and owners of this corporation. It will simply mean that business will be done through this company instead of by it. It will mean, however, loss of payroll for the workmen, and loss of purchasing power for the many things required to maintain operations, to say nothing of the purchasing power of the workmen's families.
Yours very truly,
R. J. Magor,
President.
April 21, 1924.

Have our Liberal friends so soon forgotten the proposed reciprocity pact that sounded the death knell of the Laurier government? Even under that agreement we were to get something in return for what we gave, but the present Prime Minister (Mr. Mackenzie King) and his government, in the largeness of their hearts, would give all, even of our rich heritage, and ask nothing in return from our American neighbors, not even a mess of pottage.
Before I sit down I want to ask the government to consider the budget carefully before putting it into effect. I am well acquainted with the manufacturers in the city of Hamilton and while I know that there are some firms that are making between 5 and 10 per cent, I can assure the blouse that they are only a very small minority; the large majority of the manufacturers in that city are not able to do more than come out even. I believe, as a matter of fact, that if the balance were struck as between all the profits which the manufacturers in Hamilton make and the losses that are sustained by others it would be found that the average profit would not amount to more than 3 or 4 per cent. That being the case, what will happen if the budget which the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) has presented to parliament this session is put into force? I must admit, Mr. Speaker, that I found it difficult to follow the hon. member for Hamilton (Mr. Stewart) in the sonorous speech which he addressed to himself! However, as a good Liberal, I wish to congratulate him on the worthy effort he made in trying to criticize the present administration. Moreover, in keeping with custom, the inadequacy of the arguments of the opposition members shows the weakness of their cause. Although it is part of the duty of the opposition to criticize the government, I think,
if these gentlemen in the minority do not share our views as regards the lowering of duty on instruments of production, they might have shown proof of far more sincerity by congratulating us for having decreased the national debt by $30,000,000 and reduced the taxes which burdened the people, by $24,000,-
000.	On the contrary,'they reproach us with having been false to our pledges of last year, because we did not lower the duty on farm implements, and this year we are taunted for not having lived up to our pledges, because we have lowered them.
These gentlemen preach economy; we are always glad to receive advice on economy, because it is a- virtue which we practise; however, it does not become the Conservatives, who caused the country to run into debt for hundreds of millions, to lecture us, especially when we are aware that even after the war, in 1919, they showed a deficit of $382,000,000, in other words, that the increase of the public debt in that year was greater by $50,000,000 than the *whole debt of Canada previous to the war. This, however, is not to be compared with 1920 when the deficit rose to $674,000,000; these gentlemen who are not satisfied with a decrease of $30,000,000 on the public debt, had run the country into debt for more than a billion dollars during the last two years of their administration. In my opinion, Sir, a budget which shows a reduction in the national debt and decreases the taxes certainly deserves our approval. This budget equally protects the basic industries which help the development of our national resources, such as agriculture, lumbering, mining and our fisheries, and it will benefit our farmers, labouring classes and manufacturers.
There is no denying it, the farming class has passed through hard times during the last three years. Not only have the crops been poor, but, moreover, the prices of farm products fell to previous war levels, while the farmers are forced to pay for what they need, the same prices as during the war, Further, the farmers sell their products on every market, thus competing against the farmers of the whole world, even on their own markets. In no way do they benefit from protection, for when they purchase what is needed for their farms and themselves they must buy on a protected market and pay exorbitant prices. The farmer is tired of this state of things and his position has become intolerable. This is why many have been obliged to leave their farms, and others are on the brink of bankruptcy. I congratulate the government for having taken an interest in their fate.
The present budget will be a great help to the labourer, and I am sorry to see the old
The Budget-Mr. Fajard

Tory tactics crop up again which, consists in sowing division and prejudicing the classes against one another.
The farmer 'is the friend of the labourer -whom he needs-as the labourer is the friend of the farmer, who feeds him. The latter is one of those who desires most the success of the farming class, since it is upon this class that hinges the success of the industry of which the labourer is in need.
You try to prejudice the people by telling them that the East is sacrificed to the West. The latter has received no special favour; the duties on instruments of production have not only been lowered for the West, but they have been lowered from the Atlantic to the Pacific. The people who are the most protected by the present budget are the industrial classes.
When an architect replaces another to supervise the erection of an important building, which will serve as a monument to future generations, he must first ascertain the strength of its foundations, and, if he thinks that his predecessor has made errors, it is his duty to discontinue the work and take the necessary time to repair what might-become disastrous to the whole building.
The Liberal party's architect, the Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, before proceeding to carry out in this country the policy of Laurier, observed that, since 1911, numerous rents had appeared in- our economic system, rents due to the war and far more to the bad administration of our predecessors.

The boot and shoe industry is somewhat affected by the British preference; on the other hand, how can the manufacturers complain, when the United States market which is unlimited is open to them wuthout any protection whatever? The working classes are not blind, Sir, and when they see manufacturers paying two dollars for a raw hide, they cannot help noticing that boots at $7 and $8. a pair represent a profit which they in no way benefit by. We, who hail from the country, all wish to see the welfare of the workman and manufacturer, as we wish for the success of the farmer. The rural districts are directly interested in industries, for it is with our small savings which automatically find their way towards the industrial centres, by means of the banking system, that most of the industries are kept alive. I might even add that it is one of the causes of the straitened circumstances of the farming, class. Formerly, it was an easy matter for farmers to borrow in their own parishes; but, for several years past, money is loaned on municipal and school debentures, yes, even, on industrial debentures, which are sometimes more or less doubtful. investments. This state of affairs is one more reason to state that farming is the true foundation of industry and that it was urgent to help it through the difficult crisis which it is experiencing. I, therefore, think that the banks could be more generous when it is a case of helping the farmer, and more careful than they are in their dealings with the speculator.

If an inventory was taken of money lost by banks in our old province of Quebec, we could establish that 99 per cent of these losses arise from money loaned to speculators who do not have -or barely so-any other security to offer, than their cleverness in obtaining funds.
When the manufacturer bewails the fate of the poorly paid workman, to justify a request for higher protection, he lacks sincerity; for when certain companies were realizing, during the war, profits of 25, 50 and even

100 per cent, the manufacturers did not raise the salary of the workman, on the contrary they even increased their capital fourfold in "watered stock" so as not to show too large a dividend.
I am aware that a very high tariff may have for its effect the accumulating of colossal fortunes, but it is a policy which in no way helps the revenues of the country, on the contrary, it paralyses industry which needs to be stimulated through competition. I am aware that industries which are affected by the lowering of the tariff may experience a certain set back, but this will be more than compensated by the number of small industries which will spring up, built on sound foundations, not over capitalized, and which can more easily sustain the shock of industrial crises than Some of our large industries that owe their existence to the trust placed in them or even sometimes to the friendship of bank directors. It is not from want of protection that the country suffers-for it is under the protective system that our people emigrated to the United States-it is for want of population. After the war, the shell manufacturers organized so as to supply various products, consequently our manufacturers, as at present outfitted could supply a population of 25,000,000 inhabitants. This is one of the reasons which induces me to favour immigration providing it is the right kind. This policy is an excellent thing to help in decreasing out national debt, and, it will afford us the occasion of developing our natural resources, as intended by the government.

Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) regarding his policy fcr curtailing the geodetic and topographic surveys, and I trust he may somewhat alter his plans. I should like to tender my congratulations to the Acting Minister of Finance (Mr. Robb) on the deliverance of his first budget, the manner of delivery and the substance. If we can take the information given by the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) as the correct intimation to the manufacturers that this is the beginning of the end of protection, I think we in this part of the House will hope that that prophecy is only too true. Some of our friends to the right of us have been saying that this is no time for a tariff revision. I must take exception to that statement for this reason: We remember the year 1896, when the government which was returned to power was returned on the platform of "tariff revision downwards." The question was again fought in 1911 and again in 1921. The number of us who are sitting at this end of the chamber who were elected in 1921, werp elected, perhaps, to see that the tariff policy which was being advocated by those who are to your right, Mr. Speaker, would be carried out. We find, through the press and from many speakers to the right of us here, that we are being given credit for forcing this. I am not saying or claiming that we deserve the credit; but if this is the case, we feel that we have done one of the things that the people who sent us here asked us to do. We believe that in 1921 the question of tariff revision was prominently before the people. In that connection I remember in my riding a placard or poster which was posted in some of the halls. On this poster was this:
The Americans have passed the Fordney bill to shut out Canadian products.
The next line was:
If the Progressives are elected to power, they will so lower the tariff bars that we shall be flooded with cheap American goods.
Those two statements are not consistent and some of the arguments that were put forward 
last night from that corner of the House are as inconsistent as that.
I want to touch on a few different points. I represent a constituency, in which, possibly 95 per cent of the people are engaged in dairying. The people in that constituency have been blessed with a very fertile so?/. The farmers there have had the advantage of a good education, and if I do say so. I believe they are a good average class of farmers with, perhaps, above the average quality of soil. Those farmers are today in a very depressed condition due to the market value of their products. Some hon. members claim that by this lowering of the tariff the manufacturers will go out of business. I think the hon. member for Dufferin (Mr. Woods) stated in this House a few days ago the amount of capital invested in manufacturing concerns and the amount of capital invested in agriculture, and he showed that the amount invested in agriculture was almosl double the amount invested in manufacturing concerns. While none of us wishes to see those manufacturing concerns go out of business, if they are up against it, I want to tell them that .there are farmers in Ontario who are up against it also. In the constituency from which I come we have the Finch dairy station, a station which was started by the government. I have the report for the year 1923 which shows that each farmer sending milk to the Finch dairy station-and the report takes an average of thirty farmers- produced that year 72,918 pounds of milk. At the present time cheese is selling on the market for 13^ cents per pound.

speechtext:
If the hon. member will wait a moment I will explain my position. We did not expect that the fiscal policy of this country would be changed in a minute. We, are willing to back up any government, and we would be only too pleased to back up our friends to the right if they proposed something along the line of our own platform. Unfortunately, however, they have got so far into the rut that I am afraid they will never do it.
What I have predicted about the vote of the hon. member for St. John and Albert will, I believe, be fulfilled and I maintain that that vote goes to tax goods that will come into his port. So far as we in this comer of the House are concerned we do not look upon this budget as a finality. We believe that the government in going as far as they did this year should be encouraged, but we want to make it very plain that we do not believe that this is the end, and we do not want it
to be the end. When the hon. Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart) said that this was the death-knell of protection he voiced the sentiment of hon. members in this corner of the House. In their speeches last week the whole tenor of the remarks of some hon. members was that they were afraid that this was the beginning of the end of protection, and I hope they were prophets also. It is not so much what this budget is doing as what budgets which follow will do, and the present government will be well advised to do what the majority of the people of this country are expecting them to do, namely, make a great deal more reduction in the tariff another year.
We in this corner of the House have been .taunted with having been bought and sold, with being the overflow of the Liberal party, and so on, I may say to my hon. friends that we do not believe the people put them in here as our official guardians. We will do what we think is right and the people will hold us responsible; we will go back and face our constituents and accept the responsibility.
I see that the hour for adjournment is approaching, and I shall not take up very much more of the time of the House except to pay this: The people who are defending the manufacturers to-day have, of course, a perfect right to do so, but I believe that we also have a right to defend the people who sent us here. Now as far as agriculture m this country is concerned we are in this condition; unless we get relief and can find better markets for ,our produce the exodus from the farms of this country is going to increase instead of decrease. I am going to go a little bit further, and say that I do not believe that all the ills of the farmer are going to be cured by legislation. I believe that this lowering of the tariff is going to help us, but I believe that ,we must also help ourselves in the marketing of our goods. For centuries the people of this country have been learning how to produce, and for perhaps the last ten or fifteen or twenty years we have been told how to produce by people who knew no more about it perhaps than the man in the moon. We have to-day a great expense on our experimental farms along the line of greater production and my advice to the present Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) would be to cut out a great deal of this expenditure and spend more on the development of our markets.
The hon. member for Parkdale (Mr. Spence) last night told us that he would have no truck or trade with the Yankees unless there was some money in it. I do not think it makes any difference to the people of this
1720	COMMONS
The Budget-Mr. Elliott (Dundas)
country, when they want to buy goods, who makes them so long as they can get them at a satisfactory price and the goods suit them. There is no reason why the people of this country should spend one dollar in the United States unless they believe they are getting value for their money. There is a market which the people of this country in 1911 turned down, due to a campaign not appealing to the people's common sense at all, but to their passions and sentiments. That market was turned down, and the statement has been made in this House that it is now closed to us. Now I am going to give you an example of how a factory in our own district is doing business in the United States to-day in spite of the high protection they have on dairy products entering that country, and making more money for the producer than we can get in our home market. A skimming plant was started in our town, and the cream is being shipped into the city of New York. This cream has to pay a tariff rate of 20 cents a gallon. That will net the farmers in that district to-day about thirty cents a hundred more than the milk producers are getting from the local cheese factories. There is an example of how even with this high rate of duty we can make more money dealing with the United States than we can in this much lauded home market of ours.
In conclusion, I am going to say this: According to the speeches that have been made by our Conservative friends, we are being given credit for the concessions made in this budget. We are not egotistical enough to think that we have pulled them over at all, but if such is the case, we can feel satisfied that we have done something for the betterment of Canadians generally.
